short: Nero's sprawling palace-park, built on land cleared by the fire of 64, defined his reputation for excess.
full:
After the great fire of 64 CE burned through much of central Rome, Nero appropriated a huge tract of cleared land between the Palatine, Esquiline and Caelian hills for a new residence, the Domus Aurea or Golden House. Building proceeded fast even by Roman standards, largely complete within four years by Nero's death in 68 CE. The complex combined pavilions, colonnades, an artificial lake and landscaped grounds with striking interiors, including an octagonal domed dining room whose concrete dome, pierced by a central oculus, anticipated the engineering later used in the Pantheon.

Contemporaries treated the scale of the project as proof of Nero's tyranny, and his successors moved quickly to erase it. Vespasian drained the lake to build the Colosseum on its site, and Trajan later buried the surviving rooms under the foundations of his own baths. The buried halls, rediscovered by accident in the fifteenth century, preserved wall paintings that influenced Renaissance decoration, ironically giving Nero's most reviled building a long afterlife as an artistic model.
